title: US Open Epic: Shelton Upsets Alcaraz in Latest Finish in Tournament History
summary: In a match that will be remembered for years, Ben Shelton defeated Carlos Alcaraz in a five-set thriller at the US Open, ending at 3:34 AM local time—the latest finish in the tournament's 145-year history. The quarter-final on Arthur Ashe Stadium lasted four hours and 28 minutes, with a crowd that refused to leave despite the late hour. Shelton, the eighth seed, won 6-7 (5-7), 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 7-6 (10-7) in a contest filled with breathtaking rallies and incredible athleticism. "That was a war, an epic match, so physical," Shelton said. "Carlos is one of the greatest champions in our sport already at 23 years old." This was the biggest win of Shelton's career. He had never beaten a top-three player in 17 attempts and had lost all three previous meetings with Alcaraz. But on this night, he rose to the occasion, fueled by the home crowd's support. Alcaraz, a seven-time major winner, was playing his first tournament since a wrist injury sidelined him for over four months. He had exceeded expectations by reaching the quarter-finals, but his lack of match fitness seemed to catch up with him in the high-octane encounter. Even so, he forced a deciding set and pushed Shelton to a tense 10-point match tie-break. "It was close. So I'm just not going to be disappointed about not getting the win at the end," Alcaraz said. "I'm just proud about myself, about how I fought." Shelton's victory also boosts American hopes for a first men's singles champion in New York since Andy Roddick in 2003. He will face Frances Tiafoe in an all-American semi-final on Friday, guaranteeing a home finalist.
why_it_matters: Shelton's breakthrough matters beyond one late-night match: it gives American teenagers a homegrown star at a Grand Slam and shows how injuries, conditioning, and mental toughness decide elite sport at the highest level.

background_read: The US Open is one of tennis's four Grand Slam tournaments, held every year in New York, and its main court is Arthur Ashe Stadium, named after Arthur Ashe, the first Black man to win multiple men's singles Grand Slam titles.
Shelton, an American player in his early twenties, had never beaten a top-three opponent in 17 previous attempts, making this quarter-final by far the biggest test of his young career.
Alcaraz, the 23-year-old Spanish player who has already won seven major singles titles, was returning from a wrist injury, so simply reaching the final eight was already a strong comeback.
Andy Roddick was the last American man to win the US Open in 2003, which helps explain why an all-American semi-final feels especially significant to home fans.

A finish near 3:34 AM is extreme even by US Open standards; long five-set matches, night sessions, and television scheduling all push late starts, but they also raise questions about how much recovery time players get between rounds.

perspectives.description: For Shelton and his team, the win is a career breakthrough: he had never beaten a top-three player and had lost all three prior meetings with Alcaraz. It validates his physical preparation and lifts American men's tennis, which has been waiting for a homegrown US Open champion for two decades.

From Alcaraz's side, the loss shows how brutally hard it is to return from a wrist injury straight into Grand Slam-level play. His lack of match fitness likely cost him in a four-and-a-half-hour physical battle, and the 3:34 AM finish also raises concerns about player welfare at night events.

The result fits a broader pattern: five-set tennis rewards whoever can stay freshest deepest into the match, and long layoffs after injury create real unpredictability. The result also highlights that American men, few of whom have won the US Open since Roddick in 2003, are suddenly back in the title conversation.

Shelton will face Frances Tiafoe in the all-American semi-final, meaning the United States is guaranteed a spot in the final. Whoever wins will carry enormous home expectations and could become the face of American tennis for years to come.
